task_row_model.query: In a longitudinal observational study with time-varying confounders that are themselves affected by prior treatment, how should I choose and implement an estimator to recover causal effects: compare marginal structural models estimated via inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting (IPTW) versus sequential g-estimation/structural nested models. What are the identifying assumptions for each, practical diagnostics (including when using machine learning for nuisance estimation), recommendations for weight/model specification, and guidance on software implementation and sensitivity analyses?

documents.content: Propensity score matching and cross-sectional weighting are standard for baseline confounding: estimate a treatment propensity given baseline covariates, match or weight, and then estimate mean differences. Diagnostics emphasize covariate balance (standardized mean differences), overlap plots, and trimmed samples. These approaches assume no time-varying confounding and are ill-suited to settings where covariates evolve post-treatment. While machine learning can improve propensity estimation, matching results can be unstable with high-dimensional covariates and do not address confounders that change over repeated measurements.

Structural nested mean models (SNMMs) and g-estimation identify causal effects by modelling the counterfactual mean under interventions that set treatment histories. The g-estimation procedure solves unbiased estimating equations for parameters of a SNMM using models for treatment given past covariates; it yields consistent estimates when the treatment model is correctly specified. The method is often efficient under certain SNMM parameterizations but requires detailed specification of the treatment process and is algebraically involved. Practical implementation typically demands iterative solvers and careful consideration of model fit; diagnostics focus on residuals of the treatment model and overidentification tests.

For longitudinal causal effects with time-varying confounding affected by prior treatment, marginal structural models estimated with inverse-probability-of-treatment weights (IPTW) are practical. Key identifying assumptions are sequential exchangeability (no unmeasured confounding at each time given past covariates), positivity for every treatment history, and correct temporal ordering. Estimate stabilized weights as product of numerator and denominator probabilities; use Super Learner or cross-validated ensemble learners for the numerator/denominator models, and apply cross-fitting to reduce overfitting bias. Diagnostic checks include weight distribution (mean near one, limited extreme tails), truncation sensitivity (compare estimates across truncation thresholds), effective sample size, and post-weighting covariate balance across time. Combine with outcome-model augmentation (longitudinal TMLE or doubly robust estimators) to protect against misspecification. In R, ltmle, tmle, SuperLearner and survey/ipw packages support these procedures; run sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding and explore alternative model parameterizations.

Practical advice for weight construction: compute stabilized weights using numerator models that reflect marginal treatment probabilities (possibly conditional only on baseline covariates) to reduce variance. Use flexible learners (penalized regression, random forests) for denominators but monitor positivity: visualize propensity densities by treatment over time and consider trimming or truncation at, say, the 1st and 99th percentiles. When weights are extremely variable, prefer doubly robust approaches such as longitudinal targeted maximum likelihood estimation (L-TMLE) which targets the causal parameter and can incorporate machine learning for both the outcome and treatment processes. Report effective sample size, the proportion of truncated weights, and sensitivity of point estimates to truncation and alternative learner choices.

Difference-in-differences (DiD) leverages parallel trends between treated and control units to estimate average treatment effects in panel data. The central identifying assumption is that, absent treatment, outcomes for treated and control groups would have followed the same time trend. Extensions use synthetic controls, staggered adoption adjustments, or event-study diagnostics to probe this assumption. DiD does not naturally adjust for time-varying confounders influenced by prior treatment; in such cases, specifying lead/lag dynamics or using marginal structural models may be more appropriate. Diagnostics focus on pre-treatment trend equivalence and robustness to different control sets.
